title: Slippage, partial fills, extended hours
teaches: What you lose between the price you planned and the price you got: slippage from time, size and fast markets, measured in percent and in dollars and estimated before the order; partial fills, your place in line and the order conditions that control them; and why extended-hours fills can be partial, worse or not happen at all.

sources.title: Understanding Order Types: Investor Bulletin (July 12, 2017, updated August 18, 2026)
Stop Orders: Factors to Consider During Volatile Markets (March 26, 2025)
Rule 605, Disclosure of order execution information
Rule 606, Disclosure of order routing information
3 Order Types: Market, Limit, and Stop Orders (June 11, 2024)
5 Elements of a Smart Trade Plan (October 23, 2024)
Understanding an ETF's spreads and volumes (ETF.com article on Fidelity's Learning Center)
StockCharts Insider: Why Position Sizing Sometimes Matters More Than Stock Picking (Karl Montevirgen, 2026-05-29)
sources.why_reliable: A StockCharts.com editorial article (StockCharts Insider), not ChartSchool; the author's bio on the page says he holds FINRA Series 3 and Series 34. Cited here only for the general sizing method (risk per trade divided by risk per share), which Schwab's trade-plan article (s14) states the same way.

facts.quote: Many investors who trade through online brokerage accounts assume they have a direct connection to the securities markets, but they don't.
facts.claim: Your online order does not connect you straight to the market.

facts.quote: When you push that enter key, your order is sent over the Internet to your broker -- who in turn decides which market to send it to for execution.
facts.claim: Your order goes to your broker first, and the broker picks the market that executes it.

facts.quote: Because price quotes are only for a specific number of shares, investors may not always receive the price they saw on their screen or the price their broker quoted over the phone.
facts.claim: A quote covers only a set number of shares, so you may not get the price you saw on your screen.

facts.quote: By the time your order reaches the market, the price of the stock could be slightly -- or very -- different.
facts.claim: Price can move while your order travels to the market.

facts.quote: Of course, the additional time it takes some markets to execute orders may result in your getting a worse price than the current quote - especially in a fast-moving market.
facts.claim: Extra time to execute can mean a worse price than the quote, especially in a fast market.

facts.quote: The price at which a market order will execute often deviates from the last-traded price or “real time” quote due to the demand for a stock and the prices of available liquidity at the time of execution.
facts.claim: A market order often fills away from the last price or the live quote, because of demand and the liquidity available.

facts.quote: In addition, parts of a large market order may execute at different prices due to lack of liquidity at a price at the time of execution.
facts.claim: A large market order can fill at several prices when one price lacks enough shares.

facts.quote: When the stop price is reached, a stop order becomes a market order.
facts.claim: Once the stop price is hit, a stop order is a market order.

facts.quote: The execution price an investor receives for this market order can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the demand for a stock and the prices of available liquidity.
facts.claim: A triggered stop can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: A buy limit order can only be executed at the limit price or lower, and a sell limit order can only be executed at the limit price or higher.
facts.claim: A buy limit never pays more than its limit; a sell limit never takes less.

facts.quote: Day orders, if not executed, generally cancel at the end of regular trading hours of the trading day that they are entered and will not carry over to the extended hours session or the next trading day.
facts.claim: An unfilled day order generally cancels at the end of the regular session and does not carry over.

facts.quote: An IOC order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed immediately. Any portion of the order that cannot be filled immediately will be canceled.
facts.claim: Immediate-or-cancel fills what it can at once and cancels the rest.

facts.quote: An FOK order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed immediately in its entirety; otherwise, the entire order will be canceled
facts.claim: Fill-or-kill must fill completely at once, or the whole order is canceled.

facts.quote: An AON order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed in its entirety, or not executed at all.
facts.claim: All-or-none fills the whole order or nothing.

facts.quote: However, unlike the FOK order, an AON order that is not executed immediately will remain active until it is executed or it is canceled.
facts.claim: Unlike fill-or-kill, an all-or-none order that can't fill at once stays active until it fills or is canceled.

facts.quote: Extended-hours trading systems are not linked together.
facts.claim: The systems that trade in extended hours are not linked to each other.

facts.quote: These price differences may result in you receiving an inferior price on an extended-hours stock purchase or sale.
facts.claim: Because those systems aren't linked, you may get a worse price in extended hours.

facts.quote: In addition, certain existing mechanisms that address volatility in specific stocks or in the market as a whole may be limited or not available during extended-hours trading.
facts.claim: Some volatility safeguards may be limited or missing in extended hours.

facts.quote: Investors should check with their brokerage firms to see whether orders not executed during extended-hours trading will be cancelled or whether they will be automatically entered when regular trading hours begin.
facts.claim: Brokers differ on whether unfilled extended-hours orders cancel or move into the regular session.

facts.quote: Investors should note that many of the extended-hours traders are professional traders who, by nature of their profession, generally have access to more information than individual investors.
facts.claim: Many extended-hours traders are professionals with more information than individual investors.

facts.quote: The reduced level of trading interest in extended-hours trading generally results in wider spreads between the bid and ask prices for a stock or no quotes at all.
facts.claim: Extended hours usually means wider spreads, or no quote at all.

facts.quote: The prices of some stocks traded during extended-hours trading may not reflect the prices of those stocks during regular hours, either at the end of the regular trading session or upon the opening of regular trading the next business day.
facts.claim: Extended-hours prices may not match the close or the next morning's open.

facts.quote: in some cases the price quoted to you at the time of the sale may not exactly match the price you pay for your securities.
facts.claim: The price you pay can differ from the price you were quoted.

facts.quote: This can happen because quotes may be delayed, trades take time to execute and, in highly volatile markets, millions of shares can trade in microseconds causing price swings.
facts.claim: Delayed quotes, the time a trade takes and fast markets cause that difference.

facts.quote: if you place your order before or after normal trading hours, consider the possibility that news events or other factors might significantly impact the price of the security when the market opens again.
facts.claim: News that comes out while the market is closed can move the price a lot by the next open.

facts.quote: This means you're guaranteed to get your limit price or a better price if your order is executed.
facts.claim: A limit order that fills gets your limit price or better.

facts.quote: If the market’s moving fast, you could receive less—and potentially significantly less—than $50 per share by the time your order is executed.
facts.claim: In a fast market, a sell stop at $50 can fill well below $50.

facts.quote: As a result, your order may be executed partially or not at all. If it's executed, it might not be at a competitive price compared to regular trading hours.
facts.claim: In extended hours, your order may fill in part or not at all, and the price may be worse than in the regular session.

facts.quote: Because fewer trades occur during extended hours, stocks might be vulnerable to wider swings.
facts.claim: With fewer trades in extended hours, stocks can swing more.

facts.quote: The pricing dynamics at market open might differ from the prior extended-hours trading session, which creates the risk that the price you receive during the extended-hours period might be worse than during the following day’s regular trading hours.
facts.claim: An extended-hours fill can be worse than the price the next regular session offers.

facts.quote: They might only accept limit orders during extended-hours trading and may have different policies regarding whether unexecuted extended-hours trades are canceled or carried over to the start of regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Brokers' policies differ on whether unfilled extended-hours orders are canceled or carried over.

facts.quote: The difference between estimated transactions costs and actual transactions costs. The difference usually represents revisions to price difference or spread and commission costs.
facts.claim: Slippage is the gap between the trading cost you expected and the cost you actually paid.

facts.quote: This section requires market centers, brokers, and dealers to make available standardized, monthly reports of statistical information concerning their order executions.
facts.claim: Rule 605 requires monthly statistical reports on how orders were executed.

facts.quote: Every broker or dealer shall make publicly available for each calendar quarter a report on its routing of non-directed orders in NMS stocks
facts.claim: Rule 606 requires every broker to publish a quarterly report on where it routed orders.

facts.quote: the net aggregate amount of any payment for order flow received
facts.claim: The Rule 606 report includes the payment for order flow the broker received.

facts.quote: Slippage occurs when a trade is executed at a different price than expected, often due to market movement or liquidity conditions. It can increase trading costs or reduce proceeds.
facts.claim: Slippage is a fill at a different price than expected, often from market movement or thin liquidity; it raises costs or cuts proceeds.

facts.quote: Rule 606 reports provide a breakdown of these destinations, helping investors see which venues handle the majority of their trades.
facts.claim: A Rule 606 report shows which venues handled a broker's orders.

facts.quote: Note, even if the stock reached the specified limit price, the order may not fill because there may be orders ahead of yours.
facts.claim: A stock can trade at your limit without filling you, because orders ahead of yours fill first.

facts.quote: (Limit orders are generally executed on a first-come, first-served basis.)
facts.claim: Limit orders at one price generally fill first come, first served.

facts.quote: A limit order may fill only in part (or not at all) before the session ends.
facts.claim: In extended hours, a limit order may fill only in part, or not at all.

facts.quote: it can also result in multiple executions to fill a single order, especially if the security is thinly traded.
facts.claim: An order left working across sessions can fill in several pieces, especially in a thinly traded stock.

facts.quote: There is no guarantee that execution of a stop order will be at or near the stop price.
facts.claim: A stop order may fill away from the stop price.

facts.quote: Start with the difference between the entry price, $67, and the exit price, $57, or $10, then divide the amount the trader is willing to lose, $750, by that difference to determine the number of shares
facts.claim: Risk per share is entry minus stop, and the share count is the dollars at risk divided by it.

facts.quote: Limit orders for more than 100 shares or for multiple round lots (200, 300, 400, etc.) may be filled completely or in part until completed.
facts.claim: A limit order for more than 100 shares can fill in parts.

facts.quote: there can be no assurance that all orders at a particular price limit (including yours) will be filled when that price is reached.
facts.claim: When a price is reached, not every order at that limit, yours included, is sure to fill.

facts.quote: All or none (fill the whole order or no part of it).
facts.claim: All-or-none fills the whole order or no part of it.

facts.quote: Immediate or cancel (fill the whole order or any part immediately, and cancel any unfilled balance).
facts.claim: Immediate-or-cancel fills any part at once and cancels the rest.

facts.quote: If all or part of your order is not executed by the time you’ve selected for expiration, your order will be canceled.
facts.claim: When a day order expires, any part not filled is canceled.

facts.quote: Orders are first prioritized according to price, with the orders at the same price ranked based on the order entry time.
facts.claim: In Fidelity's extended-hours sessions, orders line up by price first, then by entry time, within each market center.

facts.quote: Keep in mind that news stories and related announcements, coupled with lower liquidity and higher volatility, may cause an exaggerated and unsustainable effect on the price of a security.
facts.claim: News plus thin, volatile extended-hours trading can push a price further than it can hold.

facts.quote: You will not, however, receive an execution price that is worse than your established limit order for the extended-hours sessions.
facts.claim: In extended hours, you never fill worse than your limit.

facts.quote: Orders placed during Fidelity’s after-hours market sessions that are not filled by the end of the session at 8:00 p.m. ET are automatically canceled, unless trading is halted prior to that time.
facts.claim: At Fidelity, unfilled after-hours orders cancel when the session ends.

facts.quote: Under SEC Rule 606, broker-dealers that route equity and option orders on behalf of customers are required to prepare quarterly reports that disclose specific information about their order routing practices
facts.claim: Rule 606 requires brokers to publish quarterly reports on how they route orders.

facts.quote: The SEC's customer disclosure rule, SEC Rule 605, requires market centers and broker-dealers with 100,000 or more customer accounts, to disclose monthly data about the quality of their trade executions.
facts.claim: Rule 605 requires monthly execution-quality data from market centers and large brokers.

facts.quote: Typically, the number of shares offered on the bid or the ask will be small—sometimes 100 shares, sometime more, but rarely a huge amount.
facts.claim: Only a small number of shares usually sits at the best bid or ask.

facts.quote: someone might be willing to sell you 100 shares of JKL at $50.10, but if you want to buy 10,000 shares, you might have to pay $50.25 or more.
facts.claim: A big order can pay more than the quoted ask, because the ask covers only so many shares.

facts.quote: If you try to buy 10,000 shares of something that only trades 100 shares per day, you could have trouble.
facts.claim: An order that is large next to a stock's daily volume is hard to fill.

facts.quote: Divide your risk per trade by the risk per share, and it'll give you the number of shares to buy
facts.claim: Shares equal your risk per trade divided by your risk per share.

facts.quote: In order to prevent a partial fill, the client uses an All-or-None order type, which can also be used for stock orders.
facts.claim: An all-or-none order prevents a partial fill, on stocks too.

facts.quote: A market or limit order that must be executed at the closing price.
facts.claim: An on-close order must execute at the closing price.

facts.quote: A GTC order is an order to buy or sell a stock that lasts until it is executed in full or it is canceled.
facts.claim: A good-'til-canceled order stays working until it fills in full or is canceled.

facts.quote: During periods of heavy trading or volatility, quotes that are provided as “real time” may be stale—even if they appear not to be—and you may not receive every quote update.
facts.claim: In heavy or volatile trading, a quote labeled real time can already be stale.

facts.quote: In deciding how to execute orders, your broker has a duty to seek the best execution that is reasonably available for its customers' orders.
facts.claim: Your broker must seek the best execution reasonably available for your orders.

walkthroughs.title: The price you saw, the price you got
steps: Hit enter and your order goes to your broker first. The broker picks the market.
That trip takes time, and a quote covers only so many shares.
So your fill can land away from the quote. That gap is slippage.
Fast markets and big orders widen it. On a stop, it can cost more than you planned.

walkthroughs.title: Partial fills and your place in line
steps: A limit order can fill in part. Some shares now, the rest later or never.
Orders at one price usually fill in line, first come, first served. A trade at your limit is no promise.
All-or-none waits for the full size. Immediate-or-cancel takes what's there and cancels the rest.

walkthroughs.title: Fills outside the regular session
steps: Before the open and after the close, fewer people trade. Spreads usually widen, or quotes vanish.
Your order may fill in part or not at all. Venues aren't linked, so your price can be worse.
That price may not hold into the next open. Ask your broker whether unfilled orders cancel.

questions.q: What is slippage on a trade?
choices: Gap between expected price and fill
The bid-ask spread on the quote
The commission your broker charges
The day's high minus its low
questions.answer: Gap between expected price and fill
questions.why: The gap between the price you expected and your fill. Slippage is a fill at a different price than you expected, often from a moving market or thin liquidity.
questions.lesson_line: Slippage is the gap between the price you planned on and the price you got.

wrong.The bid-ask spread on the quote: The spread is a cost you can see before you trade. Slippage is the extra you didn't plan on.
wrong.The commission your broker charges: Commission is a fee you know before you trade. Slippage is the price itself moving away from what you expected.
wrong.The day's high minus its low: That's the day's range. It says nothing about how your own order filled.

questions.q: When you hit enter, your order goes straight to the exchange.
questions.why: False. It goes to your broker first, and the broker decides which market gets it. By the time it arrives, the price can be slightly or very different.
questions.lesson_line: Your order travels before it fills. Price can move on the way.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: When only some of the shares in your order execute, that's a ___ fill.
questions.why: Partial. Part of the order executed and the rest didn't, at least not yet. Bigger orders and thinly traded stocks are where you see it.
questions.lesson_line: Check the shares filled, not just the order status. A partial fill changes your position and your risk.

questions.q: What does an all-or-none (AON) order do?
choices: Fills the whole order or none of it
Fills what it can now, cancels the rest
Fills only at the closing price
questions.answer: Fills the whole order or none of it
questions.why: Fills the whole order or none of it. All-or-none refuses a partial fill: you get every share or no shares.
questions.lesson_line: All-or-none means no partial fill. Every share, or none.

wrong.Fills what it can now, cancels the rest: That's immediate-or-cancel. It takes a partial fill and cancels the leftover.
wrong.Fills only at the closing price: That's an on-close order. All-or-none is about how many shares fill, not when.

questions.q: An all-or-none order that can't fill right away is canceled.
questions.why: False. That's fill-or-kill. An all-or-none order that can't fill right away stays active until it fills or is canceled.
questions.lesson_line: Fill-or-kill: every share now, or cancel. All-or-none: every share, and it can wait.

questions.q: Tap the order condition that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Use ___ to take whatever shares are there right now and cancel the rest.
questions.why: Immediate-or-cancel. It fills any part it can at once and cancels whatever is left, so nothing keeps working afterwards.
questions.lesson_line: Immediate-or-cancel takes a partial fill now and leaves no order behind.

questions.q: In extended hours, many of the traders you deal with are professionals, who generally have more information than you.
questions.why: True. The SEC warns that many extended-hours traders are professionals who generally have access to more information than individual investors.
questions.lesson_line: After hours, assume the other side knows more. Name your price with care.

questions.q: Which public report shows where a broker routes its customers' stock orders?
choices: The broker's Rule 606 report
The broker's Rule 605 report
A quarterly report the SEC writes
questions.why: The Rule 606 report. Every broker must publish one each quarter on where it routed orders, including any payment for order flow it received.
questions.lesson_line: Your broker's Rule 606 report shows where it routes customer orders and what it was paid for them.

wrong.The broker's Rule 605 report: Rule 605 is the monthly report on execution quality: how orders filled. Where they went is Rule 606.
wrong.A quarterly report the SEC writes: The SEC sets the rule, but each broker publishes its own routing report.

questions.q: Your buy stop at $50.00 triggers on a breakout. You're filled at $50.40. What was your slippage, in percent?
questions.why: 0.8%. Fill minus trigger, divided by the trigger: $50.40 less $50.00, over $50.00. A triggered buy stop is a market order, and a fast breakout can fill it above the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Slippage % is the gap between fill and planned price, over the planned price. Log it on every trade.

questions.q: A stock trades about 300,000 shares a day. You want 2,000 shares. What percent of a day's volume is that? Round to two decimals.
questions.why: 0.67%. 2,000 over 300,000, rounded. Small next to a whole day, but the day never sits on the quote at once. Usually only a small number of shares shows at the best bid or ask.
questions.lesson_line: Daily volume is spread across the session. A market order meets only what's offered right now.

questions.story: A headline hits and the stock jumps. Your screen shows a $25.10 ask with 2,000 shares. You send a market buy for 300 and fill at $25.60.
questions.q: What most likely caused the higher fill?
choices: Price moved before your order arrived
The ask didn't have enough shares
Your broker added a markup
questions.answer: Price moved before your order arrived
questions.why: Price moved before your order arrived. Execution takes time, and in a fast market a real-time quote can already be stale. The size was there, so this was speed, not size.
questions.lesson_line: In a fast market, the quote you see may already be gone. A limit caps what you pay.

wrong.The ask didn't have enough shares: 2,000 shares showed at $25.10 and you wanted 300. Size wasn't the problem; time was.
wrong.Your broker added a markup: Nothing points to a markup. Your broker must seek the best execution reasonably available, and the market simply moved.

questions.q: An extended-hours order that doesn't fill always carries into the next regular session.
questions.why: False. It depends on your broker. Some cancel unfilled extended-hours orders when the session ends; others can carry them over.
questions.lesson_line: Know what your broker does with an unfilled extended-hours order before you place one.

questions.story: Your day order to buy 500 shares sits at a $30.00 limit. The stock trades at $30.00 briefly and you get 200 shares. Then it lifts to $30.60.
questions.q: What should you expect for the other 300 shares?
choices: They keep working at $30.00
They fill at $30.60 right away
They're canceled with the fill
questions.why: They keep working at $30.00. Most likely, orders ahead of yours filled first and sellers at $30.00 ran out. Your 300 stay in line until they fill or the day order ends.
questions.lesson_line: A partial fill leaves the rest working at your price. Know what's still live.

wrong.They fill at $30.60 right away: A buy limit never pays more than $30.00. The 300 wait at your price.
wrong.They're canceled with the fill: A plain limit order keeps working after a partial fill. Only a condition like immediate-or-cancel kills the rest.

questions.q: Your day limit order to buy 1,000 shares has 400 filled by the close. What happens to the other 600?
choices: They cancel at the close
They carry over to tomorrow
They fill at the closing price
questions.why: They cancel. A day order generally cancels at the end of the regular session, and any part not filled is canceled. You keep the 400.
questions.lesson_line: A day order's unfilled shares die at the close. Re-enter only if the plan still holds.

wrong.They carry over to tomorrow: That's a good-'til-canceled order. A day order doesn't carry over to the next trading day.
wrong.They fill at the closing price: Nothing turns them into a closing order. They simply cancel when the day order ends.

questions.q: You hold 500 shares. Your sell stop at $38.00 fills at $37.70 in a fast drop. What did slippage cost you, in dollars?
questions.why: $150. $38.00 less $37.70, times 500 shares. A triggered stop is a market order, and a fast drop can fill it below the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger, not a price. Slippage times shares is real money.

questions.q: Offers: 400 at $25.00, 600 at $25.05, 1,000 at $25.10. Your 2,000-share market buy takes all three. Slippage vs $25.00, in percent?

args.expr: ((a * pa + b * pb + c * pc) / (a + b + c) - pa) / pa * 100

questions.why: 0.26%. Average your fill across the three prices, weighting each by its shares, then compare it with the $25.00 you saw.
questions.lesson_line: Read the offers before you send size. You can estimate slippage before you click.

questions.story: After weak earnings you place an after-hours limit to sell 1,000 shares at $45. Only 300 fill. Your broker cancels unfilled extended-hours orders when the session ends.
questions.q: What do you hold going into the next morning?
choices: 700 shares, with no sell order working
No shares; the rest sells at the open
700 shares, still offered at $45
questions.answer: 700 shares, with no sell order working
questions.why: 700 shares, and nothing working to sell them. In extended hours a limit order may fill only in part, and this broker cancels the rest when the session ends.
questions.lesson_line: After an extended-hours fill, check what you still hold and what's still working. Then decide again.

wrong.No shares; the rest sells at the open: Nothing sells the 700 unless you enter a new order. The leftover was canceled, not sent to the open.
wrong.700 shares, still offered at $45: This broker cancels unfilled extended-hours orders at the session end. The $45 offer is gone.

questions.story: A stock trades about 300,000 shares a day. You hold 2,000 shares with a sell stop at $18.00. Bad news hits and it drops through $18 fast. Only 300 shares show on the bid.
questions.q: What should you expect from your stop?
choices: Fills at several prices below $18
All 2,000 sold at exactly $18.00
It waits for buyers to return to $18
It turns into a limit order at $18
questions.why: Fills at several prices below $18. Your stop became a market order. With only 300 shares bid, expect the rest to fill at lower bids.
questions.lesson_line: In a thin name, a stop can't promise your price. Size so a bad fill still fits your risk.

wrong.All 2,000 sold at exactly $18.00: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised price. A fast drop fills you lower.
wrong.It waits for buyers to return to $18: A triggered stop is a market order. It doesn't wait; it sells into whatever bids are there.
wrong.It turns into a limit order at $18: That's a stop-limit. A plain stop becomes a market order.

questions.q: In extended hours, you get the same volatility safeguards as in the regular session.
questions.why: False. The SEC says some mechanisms that address volatility may be limited or not available in extended hours. With fewer trades, swings can run wider.
questions.lesson_line: Out of hours, fewer guardrails and fewer traders. Price and size your orders for that.

questions.q: You'll risk $400. Your stop is $1.00 below entry, and in this thin name you expect stop fills $0.25 worse. How many shares?
questions.why: 320 shares. Divide the $400 by the stop distance plus the expected slippage, not by the stop distance alone.
questions.lesson_line: Size from the loss you'll really take, not the one you hope for.

questions.story: You plan 1,000 shares at a $40.00 limit, stop $39.00. Only 300 fill. The stock jumps, and you buy the other 700 at market for $41.20.
questions.q: What is your total risk to the $39.00 stop now?
questions.why: $1,840. The 300 shares risk $40.00 down to $39.00. The 700 you chased risk $41.20 down to $39.00. That's far past the risk you planned.
questions.lesson_line: A partial fill is just a smaller trade. Chase the rest and your risk balloons.

wrong.$1,000: That's the risk you planned, with all 1,000 shares at $40.00. You paid $41.20 for 700 of them.
wrong.$2,200: That prices all 1,000 shares at $41.20. Only 700 cost that; 300 filled at $40.00.
wrong.$300: That counts only the first 300 shares. The 700 you chased carry risk too.

questions.story: A stock closes at $80. At 4:05 p.m. it beats earnings and trades $88 after hours on thin volume. The quote is wide.
questions.q: You buy with a limit at $88.50. What does the limit protect you from?
choices: Paying more than $88.50 a share
Paying more than tomorrow's open
Getting only part of your order
questions.why: Paying more than $88.50 a share. A buy limit fills at your limit or lower, extended hours included. It can't make an after-hours price hold into the open, or promise a full fill.
questions.lesson_line: After-hours prices on news can overshoot. Your limit caps the price, not the risk.

wrong.Paying more than tomorrow's open: A limit can't do that. An after-hours price may not hold into the regular session, and news on thin volume can push a price too far.
wrong.Getting only part of your order: A limit can't promise a full fill. In extended hours an order may fill in part, or not at all.

conflicts: Rule 605 scope and timing: the SEC's 2024 amendments extend Rule 605 to brokers with 100,000 or more customer accounts. Release 34-104147 (Sept 30, 2025, read via WebFetch on sec.gov) moved the compliance date from December 14, 2025 to August 1, 2026, and the current eCFR text (up to date as of 11/05/2026, s8) carries the amended rule, as does Fidelity's page (f57). An April 1, 2026 exemptive order (34-105136) was not read. q08 only says Rule 605 is the monthly execution-quality report, which holds under the old and new rule alike.

Unfilled extended-hours orders: the SEC (f19) and FINRA (f31) say brokers differ; Fidelity cancels them at the session end (f55); Schwab's article says after-hours orders are good only for their session unless placed as GTC with extended hours. q12 is keyed False on the word 'always' and its why says 'it depends on your broker'.

Session times are left out on purpose: F1.05 records planned 9:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. overnight sessions at Nasdaq and NYSE Arca from December 6, 2026. No question or walk-through here states an extended-hours start or end time (f55's quote mentions Fidelity's 8:00 p.m. cut-off, but no member-facing text repeats it).

Slippage definitions: Nasdaq's glossary (f32) frames slippage as estimated vs actual transaction cost; Schwab (f36) as a fill at a different price than expected. q01 and the walk-through use 'the price you planned on vs the price you got', which fits both. Some broker and forex glossaries call a better-than-expected fill 'positive slippage'; this unit does not use that term (F1.03 teaches better-than-quote fills as price improvement).

q13 (a partial fill at your limit): the why says orders ahead of yours took the rest at $30.00, the reason Schwab (f39) and Fidelity (f47) give. A print at your price can also come from a venue your order was not resting on (an off-exchange trade); the key does not depend on which, because it asks only what happens to the unfilled 300, which keep working at the limit (Fidelity f46, SEC f10, f11).

q11 (time versus size): the story shows 2,000 shares at the $25.10 ask against a 300-share order so that size is ruled out. Fast-market fills away from a stale quote are on the SEC (f04, f05), FINRA (f24) and Fidelity (f65) pages. The broker-markup choice is a real beginner suspicion; its note rests on the SEC's best-execution line (f66) and makes no claim about any broker's actual practice.

Overlap with the sibling F10 units, written the same day: F10.01 already asks the marketable-limit breakout entry (its q07, q14), an overnight market order filling at the open (its q16, q17) and 'trades at your limit means a sure fill' (its q06). This unit dropped its own drafts of those three and asks time-versus-size slippage (q11), the mid-day remainder of a partial limit fill (q13) and an extended-hours partial fill with the rest canceled (q17) instead. F10.02 q16 already measures a gap through a stop in multiples of the planned loss, so this unit's stop questions use slippage in dollars (q15) and fills on size against a thin bid (q18). F10.03 q17 asks whether a bracket's stop covers a partial entry fill; this unit does not. F10.05 q18 uses the same two-lots-to-one-stop arithmetic as q21 here, framed as an add; q21 frames it as chasing the rest of a partial fill.

Hidden and reserve size: q16 says the market buy 'takes all three' offers, so the calc assumes only the shown offers fill it. q18 says 'expect' the rest to fill at lower bids, because unseen bids can exist.

Only IBKR's own Order Types page (s20) is used.

Day-order expiry: the SEC says day orders 'generally' cancel at the end of regular hours (f11); Fidelity lets a customer pick an earlier expiry (f50 sits in that passage). q14 says 'by the close' and its why says 'generally'.

Publishers: s18 is a 2014 ETF.com article reprinted on Fidelity's Learning Center, filed under 'Fidelity Investments' like s15 to s17, so the Fidelity pages never count as two publishers. s10 and s12 to s14 are all 'Charles Schwab'. The Nasdaq glossary (s7) sits on nasdaq.com, which the contract lists as Tier 1; q01, its only question, also cites Schwab (f36) and FINRA (f23), so the key holds whichever tier the checker gives s7.

Overlap with F1.03 and F1.05 avoided: F1.03 already asks the split market-order fill, its average price, price improvement and which order to use after hours; F1.05 asks session times, limit-only after hours, the no-NBBO rule, stops not running after hours and day orders cancelling at the close. This unit asks the remainder of a partially filled day order (q14), not an unfilled one, and the fill-side extended-hours facts F1.05 left unused (professional traders, volatility safeguards, carry-over policy, the price not holding into the next open).
